'''Cornelia Isabella''' "'''Cori'''" '''Bargmann''' (born January 1, 1961)<ref name=AAAS /> is an American [[Neurobiology|neurobiologist]]. She is known for her work on the genetic and neural circuit mechanisms of behavior using ''[[Caenorhabditis elegans|C. elegans]]'', particularly the mechanisms of [[olfaction]] in the worm. She has been elected to the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] and had been a [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]] investigator at [[University of California, San Francisco|UCSF]] and then [[Rockefeller University]] from 1995 to 2016. She was the Head of Science<ref>{{Cite web|title=Our Leadership|url=https://chanzuckerberg.com/about/leaders/|access-date=2021-04-09|website=Chan Zuckerberg Initiative|language=en-US}}</ref> at the [[Chan Zuckerberg Initiative]] from 2016 to 2022.<ref name=":2" /> In 2012 she was awarded the $1 million [[Kavli Prize]], and in 2013 the $3 million [[Breakthrough Prize in Life Sciences]].

==Early life and education==
Bargmann was born in [[Virginia]] and grew up in [[Athens, Georgia]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.kavliprize.no/binfil/download.php?tid=54638 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20131203031458/http://www.kavliprize.no/binfil/download.php?tid=54638 |url-status=dead |title=The Kavli Prize: "Cornelia Bargmann" |archivedate=December 3, 2013}}</ref> Her parents are European immigrants.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal |last1=Neill |first1=Ushma S. |title=A conversation with Cornelia Bargmann |journal=Journal of Clinical Investigation |date=2 July 2018 |volume=128 |issue=7 |pages=2655–2656 |doi=10.1172/JCI122804 |pmid=30108194 |pmc=6025965 }}</ref> She is one of four sisters and the daughter of Rolf Bargmann, a statistician and computer scientist at the [[University of Georgia]].<ref name="Crevar">Crevar.</ref> She grew up playing the piano and was exposed to literature and education from a very young age. She described her family as “frighteningly well educated”.<ref name=pmid15728356>{{cite journal |last1=Marino |first1=M. |title=Biography of Cornelia I. Bargmann |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |date=22 February 2005 |volume=102 |issue=9 |pages=3181–3183 |doi=10.1073/pnas.0500025102 |pmid=15728356 |pmc=552904 |doi-access=free }}</ref> She was inspired to study science because her older sister attended medical school. She also says that growing up in the space era fostered her love for science.<ref name=":0" />

She completed her undergraduate studies at the [[University of Georgia]] in 1981, with a degree in [[biochemistry]]. While at UGA, she grew her lab experience by working in the labs of Wyatt Anderson and Sidney Kushner.<ref name=pmid15728356/> She completed graduate school at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]] with a Ph.D. in the department of Biology in 1987 under the supervision of [[Robert Weinberg (biologist)|Robert Weinberg]]. She examined the molecular mechanisms of [[oncogenesis]], and helped identify the role of [[Ras (protein)|Ras]] in bladder cancer. She wrote her thesis on [[HER2/neu|neu]], a non-Ras [[oncogene]]. Although the relevance of her research was doubted at the time, it later led to significant treatments in [[breast cancer]].<ref name=pmid15728356/>

== Career and research ==
Bargmann completed a postdoc with [[H. Robert Horvitz]] at MIT, working on [[molecular biology]] mechanisms of [[neuroscience]]. She began working on chemosensory behavior in ''[[Caenorhabditis elegans|C. elegans]]'', and achieved several breakthroughs, demonstrating, among other things, that [[nematode]]s have a sense of smell.<ref name=pmid15728356/><ref>{{Cite web|date=2012-02-17|title=Features {{!}} As the Worm Turns|url=http://www.uga.edu/gm/604/FeatWorm.html|access-date=2021-04-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120217181516/http://www.uga.edu/gm/604/FeatWorm.html|archive-date=2012-02-17}}</ref>

Bargmann accepted a faculty position at [[UCSF]] in the department of Anatomy in 1995. She was promoted from assistant professor to professor in 1998, and served as vice chair of the department from 1999 to 2000.<ref name=pmid15728356/>

She continued her studies of worm behavior and neural control, focusing on [[olfaction]] at the molecular level. She looked for genes similar to those found by Richard Axel and [[Linda B. Buck|Linda Buck]] to be the basis of smell and taste, and found those genes in the recently sequenced genome of ''C. elegans''. Her work led to discoveries of the mechanisms underlying complex behaviors, such as feeding behaviors.<ref name=pmid15728356/><ref>{{Cite news|last=Wade|first=Nicholas|date=2011-06-20|title=In Tiny Worm, Unlocking Secrets of the Brain|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/06/21/science/21brain.html|access-date=2021-04-07|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> The work has continued to lead to a deeper understanding of the brain, sensory abilities, and neuronal development. Bargmann also identified [[SYG-1]], a "matchmaker" molecule that directs [[neuron]]s to form connections with each other during [[development (biology)|development]].<ref name="Friend-2003">{{cite news |last1=Friend |first1=Tim |date=March 10, 2003 |title=Nerve cell mystery is unlocked |url=https://usatoday30.usatoday.com/news/health/2003-03-10-nerve-cells_x.htm |work=USA Today }}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=Internationally renowned neurobiologist to join Rockefeller University; Cori Bargmann discovered "matchmaker" molecule|url=https://www.rockefeller.edu/news/3633-internationally-renowned-neurobiologist-to-join-rockefeller-university-cori-bargmann-discovered-matchmaker-molecule|access-date=2021-04-07|website=News|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=2005-05-08|title=UCSF News Office|url=http://pub.ucsf.edu/newsservices/releases/200307243/|access-date=2021-04-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050508042844/http://pub.ucsf.edu/newsservices/releases/200307243/|archive-date=2005-05-08}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=I Smell a ... Worm|url=https://www.the-scientist.com/reverse-transcript/i-smell-a-worm-48508|access-date=2021-04-07|website=The Scientist Magazine®|language=en}}</ref>

In 2004, Bargmann moved to [[Rockefeller University]].<ref name=":1" /> She said that the reason for the move is that she wanted more flexibility to focus on research.<ref name=":0" /> She served as an Investigator of the [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]] until 2016 before she took the President of [[Chan Zuckerberg Initiative|CZI]]. Bargmann's lab uses a relatively simple organism, the nematode ''C. elegans'', and its extremely sensitive sense of smell to study how genes regulate neuronal development, function, and behavior. Her work has been recognized with numerous awards including election to the [[National Academy of Sciences]]. She also served on the Life Sciences jury for the [[Infosys Prize]] in 2012.

Bargmann's research was funded by the [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]] from 1995 to 2016.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Cornelia I. Bargmann|url=https://www.hhmi.org/scientists/cornelia-i-bargmann|access-date=2021-04-07|website=HHMI.org|language=en}}</ref> She was the co-chair of the BRAIN initiative and the Head of Science for the [[Chan Zuckerberg Initiative]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|date=2016-09-23|title=Rockefeller neuroscientist Cori Bargmann to lead science work at Chan Zuckerberg Initiative {{!}} Newswire|url=http://newswire.rockefeller.edu/2016/09/21/rockefeller-neuroscientist-cori-bargmann-to-lead-science-work-at-chan-zuckerberg-initiative/|access-date=2021-04-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160923023355/http://newswire.rockefeller.edu/2016/09/21/rockefeller-neuroscientist-cori-bargmann-to-lead-science-work-at-chan-zuckerberg-initiative/|archive-date=2016-09-23}}</ref> She won the Breakthrough prize in Life Sciences in 2013.<ref name=":0" />

Bargmann is married to fellow olfactory scientist [[Richard Axel]], a Nobel laureate. Previously, she had been married to Michael J. Finney, who also completed graduate studies at MIT and is now a Director at Sage Science, Inc.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2011-09-30 |title=Directors {{!}} Sage Science |url=https://sagescience.com/about-us/advisors-directors/ |access-date=2025-07-15 |language=en-US}}</ref>

For a vivid portrait of Bargmann as a young scientist working in Weinberg's lab, see [[Natalie Angier]]'s book ''[[Natural Obsessions|Natural Obsessions: The Search for the Oncogene]]''.
